abstracts.value: Data-driven machine learning algorithms represent an alternative to numerical or analytical modeling of vibrating objects for the purpose of extracting their material or geometric properties. Their performance is conditioned by the quality of the training dataset, which should contain all possible production configurations of the object and measurement conditions. In this work, we propose a data-augmentation method based on manipulations of the vibration properties rather than numerical signal post-processing. Instead of modifying the sample’s material or geometry, we connect an additional sensor and actuator to the sample and use low-latency electronics to control the feedback signal. This delivers an electromechanical system with tunable oscillation properties. This signal diversification method is demonstrated on the classification of correct and incorrect adhesion of two aluminum plates. The labeling accuracy of 67% on nine unknown test objects, when trained on a single unchangeable training object, increases to 83% when the variety of the training vibration signals is augmented by varying the parameters of the electrovibratory feedback. This provides advantages for industrial quality control, where a large number of reference training samples are not available.

titles.title: Data augmentation by an electro-vibratory feedback improves signal interpretation by neural networks

abstracts.value: This dissertation presents a search for low-energy neutrinos in temporal coincidence with gravitational wave events reported by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during the fourth observing run (O4), using 499.0 days of data collected during the liquid scintillator phase of the SNO+ experiment. The search uses inverse beta decay (IBD), which is primarily sensitive to electron antineutrinos, and neutrino-proton elastic scattering, a complementary neutral current channel providing sensitivity to all neutrino flavors. Candidate events were identified using optimized reconstruction and event-selection criteria developed with Monte Carlo simulations and validated with background-only data. The IBD background rate was measured directly from data, naturally incorporating reactor antineutrinos, geoneutrinos, radioactive backgrounds, cosmogenic backgrounds, and accidental coincidences present during detector operation. A model-independent framework was developed using flat spectrum neutrino Monte Carlo samples, allowing the detector response to be evaluated as a function of neutrino energy and applied to different theoretical emission models. As part of this work, improvements were made to the SNO+ Monte Carlo simulation, including modifications to the IBD generator to produce a true flat neutrino spectrum and corrections to the implementation of the neutrino-proton elastic scattering cross section. Detector characterization studies, including measurements of the deployed scintillator light yield and investigations of detector timing and electronics performance, were also performed to validate the detector response used throughout the analysis. The final gravitational wave-coincident dataset contained 143 candidates overlapping stable SNO+ data-taking periods. After excluding candidates classified as terrestrial or unknown by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, the final astrophysical sample used for compact binary merger fluence limits contained 126 gravitational wave candidates. No statistically significant neutrino excess was observed in either the IBD or neutrino-proton elastic scattering channels. The IBD search observed no coincident candidates in the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, consistent with an expected background of 1.25 ± 0.09 events. The corresponding Feldman-Cousins 90% confidence level upper limit is N90stack = 1.47 signal events. Stacked average (per gravitational wave) upper limits on the electron antineutrino fluence were derived for both monoenergetic neutrino emission and model-dependent spectra, including thermal neutrino and core-collapse supernova-inspired models used as detector sensitivity benchmarks. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering search represents the first application of this all-flavor channel to a gravitational wave-coincident neutrino search. Using an optimized ±50 s coincidence window, 108424 candidate events were observed, consistent with the expected background of 108345 ± 786 events estimated from local sidebands. The observed 0.24σ fluctuation is consistent with the background-only hypothesis. For the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, the Feldman-Cousins method gives a 90% confidence level upper limit of N90stack = 1479.6 signal events. These results are used to derive the first all-flavor neutrino-proton elastic scattering fluence limits associated with compact binary merger candidates. The resulting SNO+ IBD fluence limits improve upon previous liquid scintillator gravitational wave-neutrino searches by approximately an order of magnitude in the few-MeV energy region, primarily due to the larger fiducial target mass, increased gravitational wave sample size, and low background rate achieved in SNO+. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering results establish the first all-flavor MeV neutrino search through this interaction channel in coincidence with gravitational wave events. Together, these analyses extend previous multi-messenger searches performed by Borexino, KamLAND, and Super-Kamiokande and demonstrate the capability of SNO+ to search for weak neutrino signals associated with astrophysical transients.

titles.title: The Search for Mev-scale Neutrinos in Temporal Coincidence With o4 Gravitational Wave Events Using the Sno+ Experiment

abstracts.value: Future high-energy proton colliders will require high-field accelerator magnets that exceed the capabilities of Nb-Ti technology. The Nb₃Sn quadrupole magnets developed for the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) upgrade represent the first large-scale application of this technology in an operational accelerator. Following an extensive short-model R&D program comprising approximately 40 coils and seven 1.5 m-long magnets, a full-scale prototyping phase established the foundation for series production. The series-fabrication phase is now approaching completion, with more than 120 coils of 4.5 m length produced by the US Accelerator Upgrade Project and more than 70 coils of 7.2 m length manufactured at CERN. This large-scale effort, distributed across multiple manufacturing sites, provides a unique opportunity to assess the scalability of Nb₃Sn technology in terms of magnet length, production volume, and manufacturing throughput. We present an overview of the production timeline, learning curve, major nonconformities, and process improvements, with a particular focus on coil fabrication.

titles.title: Scale Up in Length of Nb<sub>3</sub>Sn Accelerator Magnets: The Experience From MQXF Coils

abstracts.value: A new quench-protection technique, energy shift with coupling (ESC), has recently been proposed and shows significant promise for the protection of high-field magnets. The ESC system includes normal-conducting coils that are strongly magnetically coupled to, but galvanically insulated from, the magnet coils. When activated, the system rapidly transfers energy from the magnet to the ESC coils, substantially reducing ohmic losses at the magnet hot spot and promoting the transition of the superconducting coils to the normal state through transient losses. During the subsequent magnet-current discharge, part of the stored magnetic energy is transferred to the ESC coils. ESC was recently demonstrated successfully at CERN on a 400 mm long flat racetrack magnet structure without an aperture. In this work, we present the application of the ESC method to a subscale common-coil magnet known as the subscale stress-managed common-coil series (subSMCC2), designed and manufactured by the Magnet Development Laboratory at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The subSMCC2 is a 300 mm long magnet comprising four stress-managed Nb₃Sn common coils and is designed to reach bore and peak coil fields of approximately 5.3 T and 6.4 T, respectively, at a short-sample current of 9.5 kA. Protecting this magnet following a quench, without the use of energy extraction, is particularly challenging because of its very high stabilizer current density, exceeding 5 kA/mm². The proposed ESC-based protection scheme employs two common-coil-type ESC coils made from rectangular copper conductors and located on the outer sides of the magnet coils. Tests performed at the CERN magnet test facility successfully demonstrated the performance of the ESC system under a variety of operating conditions. These results show that ESC is an effective, high-performance quench-protection technology capable of protecting magnets operating at very high current densities.

titles.title: ESC Enables Protection of an Accelerator Superconducting Magnet With $>$5 kA/mm$^{2}$ Copper Current Density

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

titles.title: Compact High Turns Ratio Superconducting Transformer: Comparison Between Cu and REBCO Winding Materials

abstracts.value: This article investigates the mechanical characteristics and critical current performance of aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tape cable (ASTC) for the circular electron-positron collider detector magnet. In-plane bending, torsion, and uniaxial tension tests are carried out, combined by finite element analysis. The correlation between critical current and strain under different loading conditions is systematically analyzed, and key mechanical thresholds are determined. Results show that the minimum allowable in-plane bending diameter is 1200 mm. The critical twist pitch is 327 mm. The critical current degrades to 95% of the initial value when the tensile strain in the REBCO tape reaches 0.37%. This study provides essential experimental data and theoretical support for the structural design and engineering application of ASTC in high-field superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Mechanical Characteristics of Aluminium-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tape Cable for the CEPC Detector Magnet

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: The q-plate is a spatially inhomogeneous SU(2) birefringent optical element that has garnered significant interest due to its ability to mediate the spin-orbit interaction of light and facilitate the generation of structured light with singularities. The q-plate features a spatially varying fast axis orientation defined by three parameters: the topological charge q, retardance delta, and the offset angle $alpha_0$. While the parameter alpha_0 can be changed many times by rotation, any change in the charge and/or retardance entails the fabrication of a new plate. This limitation can be overcome through the concept of an effective waveplate, where multiple waveplates, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, are aligned coaxially so that, under specific constraints, the composite system emulates the behavior of a single effective waveplate. This work presents a comprehensive mathematical formalism for realizing an effective waveplate through a cascaded configuration of three q-plates, each chosen as either a quarter-wave q-plate, a half-wave q-plate, or a combination thereof. Some configurations offer tunability of the retardance over the full range from 0 to $2pi$, even though q-plates with fixed retardances of $pi/2$ and pi are used in sequence to form an effective q-plate. This feature enables holonomic polarization walk on the higher-order Poincare sphere. Such a capability holds significant potential for applications involving structured light associated with the higher-order Poincare sphere, particularly in controlled polarization transformations and polarization-topology engineering.

titles.title: Mathematics of effective q-plate in polarization optics

abstracts.value: Quantum computing (QC) emulation is critical for exploring and advancing near-term quantum algorithms, given the ongoing scalability and reliability challenges of quantum hardware. While FPGA-based QC emulators have emerged as efficient alternatives to bridge the gap toward practical quantum computers, most existing solutions depend on high-performance systems, limiting their applicability in embedded and edge environments. In this work, we present a scalable, standalone FPGA-based emulator specialized for resource-constrained systems. Our design targets the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), particularly for the Weighted-MaxCut problem. By leveraging diagonal decomposition and a pipeline-centric hardware architecture, we reduce the computational complexity of QAOA from $\boldsymbol{O(N^{2})}$ to $\boldsymbol{O(N)}$, where $\boldsymbol{N}$ $\boldsymbol{=}$ $\boldsymbol{2^{n}}$ is the state dimension for $\boldsymbol{n}$ qubits. This reformulation and its architectural co-design significantly reduces hardware overhead, enabling larger qubit configurations on edge-level FPGAs. We encapsulate these optimizations into a hardware accelerator called the Quantum MaxCut Accelerator (QMA), which integrates seamlessly into a RISC-V platform, forming a self-contained emulator. Additionally, we introduce QC Emulator eXpress (QEX), a full-stack automation framework that streamlines QMA integration into configurable RISC-V platforms, significantly facilitating rapid and scalable emulator development and deployment. Through extensive prototyping of various QAOA emulators, our experiments confirm that the proposed QMA achieves energy reductions of up to $\textbf{907}\boldsymbol{\times}$ compared to the CPU-only software baseline under the same standalone FPGA/RISC-V setting and reliably supports up to 9 qubits on a mid-tier FPGA. These results demonstrate the energy efficiency and scalability of the proposed system as a self-contained FPGA/RISC-V platform for edge-local QAOA emulation, prototyping, and HW/SW co-design exploration under resource-constrained conditions.

titles.title: Quantum at the Edge: Scalable Standalone FPGA Emulator for QAOA-Based Weighted-MaxCut

abstracts.value: Solitons are fundamental entities in nonlinear wave equations across diverse branches of physics. In systems with competing nonlinearities, a hallmark transition occurs from traditional bell-shaped profiles to flat-top configurations as the norm increases. In this work, we analyze double flat-top solitons in systems of two coupled generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equations. We develop a theoretical and variational framework that provides both physical insight and a computationally efficient description of these eigenstates. In the large-norm regime, and for a broad class of nonlinear potentials supporting flat-top states, we derive explicit analytical expressions for the plateau densities and chemical potentials, together with variational estimates for the interfacial properties characterizing the solutions. These quantities are controlled by algebraic conditions that generalize the Maxwell coexistence condition to coupled wave functions. We show that two-component flat-top solitons may form core–shell configurations, in which a two-component core is surrounded by a shell of the dominant species, as well as no-shell configurations, where both species occupy the same spatial domain. Using the cubic-quintic nonlinearity as a prototypical model, we compare these analytical predictions with direct numerical computations of the stationary states and find excellent agreement in the flat-top regime. The resulting picture admits a natural interpretation in terms of phase coexistence in an effective binary fluid, with kink-like interfaces carrying an excess grand potential that plays the role of a surface tension. This formalism is applicable to diverse physical platforms, including nonlinear optics, multicomponent Bose–Einstein condensates, and Q-ball configurations in relativistic field theories.

titles.title: Theory of double flat-top solitons in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations

When Graph Autoencoders Look the Wrong Way:
Complexity Bias and Simple Baselines in Unsupervised
Anomaly Detection on the LHC Olympics 2020 Dataset

Jamil Khan1

Independent researcher; undergraduate student in Computer Engineering
ORCID: 0009-0007-1762-0416

Abstract

Graph autoencoders (GAEs) trained only on background are a natural candidate for model-
agnostic new-physics searches. I tested two of them on the LHC Olympics 2020 R&D dataset,
where a W ′ → XY → (qq̄)(qq̄) dijet resonance is hidden in QCD background. The first is
a node-level GAE that scores per-particle reconstruction error. The second encodes the
whole event, reconstructs it with a set decoder and a Chamfer loss, and offers three scores:
reconstruction error, latent k-nearest-neighbour distance and latent Gaussian-mixture likeli-
hood. The decision criterion was fixed before looking at any test result. Neither model beats
simple label-free observables. The node-level model reaches an AUC of 0.483 ± 0.005 with
max-reduction and 0.781 with mean-reduction; all three event-level scores are inverted, with
AUCs between 0.401 and 0.436, stable across seeds, nine ablations, and signal-contaminated
training. By contrast, the mean transverse momentum per particle, ⟨pT⟩ = HT/N , reaches
0.811, and −τ21 of the leading jet reaches 0.801. Correlation and binned analyses indicate
that the latent-density scores track event complexity: the signal has fewer, harder particles
than QCD and is therefore placed in dense regions of the learned manifold. The benchmark
code is public, and I suggest ⟨pT⟩ as a standard reference baseline for unsupervised methods
on this dataset.

1 Introduction
Searches for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
are mostly designed around specific signal hypotheses. Model-agnostic anomaly detection aims
to complement them by flagging events that are atypical with respect to the Standard Model
background, without assuming a signal model. The LHC Olympics 2020 (LHCO) [1] established
a common benchmark for this task, and autoencoders, in which events with large reconstruction
error are treated as anomalous, are among the most widely studied unsupervised approaches [2–
5].

Autoencoder scores have a known weakness: they can end up measuring how complex an
input is rather than how unusual it is. For jet images, simple signal jets turn out to be easier
to reconstruct than QCD jets [4]. This project started as an attempt to build a working graph-
based detector, and ran into the same problem for particle graphs of whole events. This paper
documents what happened:

1. a reproducible benchmark harness on the public LHCO R&D data, with a frozen test set,
multi-seed runs, bootstrap confidence intervals and within-bin AUCs that test whether a
score carries information beyond trivial event quantities;

2. a set of label-free reference baselines, among which the mean transverse momentum per
particle, ⟨pT⟩ = HT/N , is the strongest particle-level observable (AUC 0.811), above HT,
mjj , and a node-level GAE;

3. a negative result, under a decision rule fixed in advance, for an event-level GAE whose three
anomaly scores are systematically inverted, with ablations, a contamination study, and a
correlation-based diagnosis that links the latent-density inversion to event complexity.

None of this is a working anomaly detector. The practical point is simpler: before claiming that
an unsupervised model has learned something on this dataset, compare it with ⟨pT⟩. If it cannot
beat a ratio of two event totals, it has probably only learned the energy and multiplicity scale.

2 Dataset and test protocol
I use the LHCO 2020 R&D dataset [1, 6]. Background consists of QCD dijet events and signal
of W ′ → XY with mW ′ = 3.5 TeV, mX = 500 GeV and mY = 100 GeV, each of X and
Y decaying to two quarks. Events were generated with Pythia 8 [7] and the Delphes 3 [8]
detector simulation, and are stored as up to 700 hadrons (pT, η, ϕ). Jet-level features (anti-kt [9]
R = 1 jet masses, N -subjettiness ratios [10] and mjj) are taken from the accompanying feature
file.

One practical warning first: the publicly available file events_anomalydetection_v2.h5 is
sorted: rows 0–999,999 are background and rows ≥ 1,000,000 are signal. Any pipeline that
reads a prefix of the file therefore sees no signal at all; I select events explicitly by row index.
The test set is frozen across all experiments: 5,000 background events (rows 40,000–44,999) and
5,000 signal events (rows 1,000,000–1,004,999). Models are trained on 180,000 background-only
events (rows ≥ 45,000) with a 20,000-event background validation set.

Metrics. I report the ROC AUC with bootstrap confidence intervals over the 10,000 test
events (95% for baselines; 98.3% for the three model scores, a Bonferroni correction for three
comparisons). To test whether a score carries information beyond trivial event quantities, I also
compute the AUC within bins of HT, particle multiplicity N , and leading-particle pT. The sign
of every score (“larger = more anomalous”) is fixed in advance.

Decision criterion. Before any test result for the event-level model, I fixed the following gate:
a model score passes only if the lower bound of its seed-averaged AUC interval exceeds the best
particle-level baseline, and its minimum within-bin AUC is at least 0.6.

3 Models
Node-level GAE. Each event is a radius graph with edges between particles at ∆R < 0.4. A
graph convolutional encoder [11] compresses each particle’s features to a one-dimensional latent
and a decoder reconstructs its standardized (pT, η, ϕ); the model has 420 effective parameters.
The event score is the maximum or the mean of the per-particle reconstruction errors.

Event-level GAE. The encoder applies three residual neighbour-averaging layers of width 64
on the same ∆R < 0.4 graph, followed by concatenated mean, max and pT-weighted pooling
into a 16-dimensional event latent. A set decoder reconstructs the K = 48 hardest particles
and is trained with a symmetric Chamfer distance [12], which is invariant to particle ordering.
Events are truncated to the 350 hardest particles, a cut chosen from the measured multiplicity
distribution before training (0.7% of background and 0.02% of signal events exceed it). The
model has 95,888 parameters and is trained for 30 epochs with AdamW (learning rate 10−3,
batch size 256, early-stopping patience 5) on one NVIDIA T4 GPU, about 18 minutes per seed.
Three anomaly scores are evaluated: (i) the Chamfer reconstruction error; (ii) the mean distance
to the 20 nearest training latents; and (iii) the negative log-likelihood of the latent under an
8-component Gaussian mixture fitted to training latents.

4.3 Ablations and contamination

Nine variations of the event-level model, each with two seeds, were run as a sensitivity analysis
and not used to select a configuration (Table 3). None produces a useful score; the best single
value is 0.502 (Chamfer, K = 24), i.e. chance. Training on background contaminated with
1% signal changes the scores by at most ∼ 0.015, which is inconclusive with one seed. At 9%
contamination, the signal fraction of the R&D file, the density scores become more inverted
(kNN 0.362, GMM 0.387), consistent with signal events making signal-like regions of the latent
space denser.

5 Diagnosis
Table 4 gives Spearman correlations of the seed-0 scores with simple event quantities. The latent-
density scores increase with multiplicity (ρ = +0.28 for kNN, +0.23 for GMM) and decrease
with ⟨pT⟩ (−0.27, −0.20), also within background alone. Their AUC within multiplicity bins is
close to chance (kNN 0.43–0.50, GMM 0.47–0.51). Since signal events have fewer and harder
particles than QCD background, they fall into dense regions of a latent space trained on QCD.
Under the pre-declared sign (far from training data means anomalous), this produces AUCs
below 0.5. This explanation is supported by correlations but was not tested causally.

The Chamfer score behaves differently: it barely tracks multiplicity (ρ = +0.08) or ⟨pT⟩
(ρ = −0.07), and remains inverted within multiplicity bins (0.41–0.48) and within HT bins
(down to 0.31). Its inversion is therefore not explained by multiplicity alone, and its origin
remains open. The three scores are only moderately correlated with one another (Chamfer–
kNN 0.53, Chamfer–GMM 0.42, kNN–GMM 0.87). Flipping the sign post hoc would give AUCs
of 0.56–0.60, still far below ⟨pT⟩. I mention this only to show that the scores contain a weak
complexity signal rather than noise; it is not a result.

6 Discussion and outlook
These results add to the evidence that autoencoder-based anomaly scores are vulnerable to
complexity bias [4], and extend it to particle-graph representations of full events. Two practical
lessons follow. First, unsupervised methods on the LHCO R&D data should be compared not

only with HT but with ⟨pT⟩, which already reaches AUC 0.81 without any training. Second,
within-bin AUCs at fixed multiplicity and HT are a cheap and informative diagnostic: a score
that loses its discrimination at fixed complexity has not learned substructure.

The features that distinguish the signal in this dataset are jet-level: two-prong substructure
(τ21), jet masses and mjj . These are not available to the encoder as explicit inputs. Natural next
steps are therefore (i) adding jet-level and substructure inputs, (ii) conditioning the model on,
or regressing out, multiplicity and ⟨pT⟩ so that the score measures structure at fixed complexity,
and (iii) choosing the score sign on background-only or simulated data. Large foundation models
for collider physics trained on simulated events are expected to face the same issue. Benchmarks
of the kind released here can be used to check whether their anomaly scores capture more than
event complexity.

Limitations. All results use a single signal model and the R&D dataset, not the LHCO black
boxes. The event-level model was evaluated in one configuration fixed in advance with limited
ablations, and the complexity explanation is correlational. Ablation and contamination runs
use two or one seeds, so differences below ∼ 0.02 should not be interpreted.

abstracts.value: Graph autoencoders (GAEs) trained only on background are a natural candidate for model-agnostic new-physics searches. I tested two of them on the LHC Olympics 2020 R&D dataset, where a W' -> XY -> (qq)(qq) dijet resonance is hidden in QCD background. The first is a node-level GAE that scores per-particle reconstruction error. The second encodes the whole event, reconstructs it with a set decoder and a Chamfer loss, and offers three scores: reconstruction error, latent k-nearest-neighbour distance and latent Gaussian-mixture likelihood. The decision criterion was fixed before looking at any test result. Neither model beats simple label-free observables. The node-level model reaches an AUC of 0.483 +/- 0.005 with max-reduction and 0.781 with mean-reduction; all three event-level scores are inverted, with AUCs between 0.401 and 0.436, stable across seeds, nine ablations, and signal-contaminated training. By contrast, the mean transverse momentum per particle, <pT> = HT/N, reaches 0.811, and -tau21 of the leading jet reaches 0.801. Correlation and binned analyses indicate that the latent-density scores track event complexity: the signal has fewer, harder particles than QCD and is therefore placed in dense regions of the learned manifold. The benchmark code is public, and I suggest <pT> as a standard reference baseline for unsupervised methods on this dataset.

titles.title: When Graph Autoencoders Look the Wrong Way: Complexity Bias and Simple Baselines in Unsupervised Anomaly Detection on the LHC Olympics 2020 Dataset

abstracts.value: A Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based Physical Layer Security (PLS) scheme (QKD-PLS) for optical fiber links is proposed and evaluated. In detail, a novel amplitude and phase scrambling technique for exploiting and seamlessly integrating high key rate QKD for the encryption of the modulation parameters of conventional complex modulation schemes like M-ary Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (M-QAM) and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is described. Scrambling is applied to both preamble (pilot signals) and payload segments of the transmission frame, to prevent the eavesdroppers from performing vital receiver functionalities such as frame synchronization and channel estimation. Additionally, a practical Key Management System (KMS) taking care of all key synchronization processes is developed and introduced. Moreover, another advantage of QKD exploitation to the proposed solution comes from the application of high entropy kbps-rate QKD keys feeding pseudo-random number generators, to modify the broadband modulation symbols in one-time pad, therefore significantly improving data protection. Experimental evaluation via a transmission scenario in fiber links is also presented, depicting the efficacy of the QKD-PLS.

abstracts.value: This paper addresses a fundamental unresolved problem in inflationary cosmology: what quantum-state structure makes the one-realization classical description used in late-time cosmology physically meaningful within unitary quantum theory? We identify a structure that supports such a description, which we call Cosmological Classical Branches (CCBs). After reheating, the curvature perturbation is a collective variable rather than an independent subsystem. This shifts the classicality problem from the reduced state of the curvature perturbation itself to records of primordial information in the post-reheating matter state. When distinct matter components respond to the same primordial realization and their conditional states become distinguishable across different realizations, they carry records of the information about the curvature perturbation. A record in one component makes the realization readable, while a compatible record in a disjoint component suppresses interference accessible to operations confined to the first component, forming CCBs. Conditioning on a physical record yields a one-realization description within a CCB, in which the resolved primordial value acts as a c-number label while the matter degrees of freedom remain quantum. We test this criterion using effective models of two radiation fluids during radiation domination and of photons and cold dark matter around radiation--matter equality. We also show that a CCB typical with respect to the primordial Born measure exhibits the expected one-realization statistics: mode averages approach the primordial two-point statistics at fixed nonzero wavenumber in the large-volume limit. Overall, these results provide an operational framework at the quantum-state level connecting the primordial quantum superposition to the one-realization cosmological history assumed in standard cosmology.

titles.title: Cosmological Classical Branches: Operational classicality of primordial curvature perturbations from late-time matter records

abstracts.value: We study zero-error communication and exact simulation of quantum channels assisted by quantum no-signalling correlations. For a channel with Kraus operator space $K$, we introduce a semidefinite programming parameter $Γ(K)$ that is exactly multiplicative under tensor products and upper-bounds $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)$, where $\log_2Θ_{\rm NS}(K)=C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ and $C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ denotes the asymptotic quantum no-signalling-assisted zero-error capacity. Among known upper bounds on $Θ_{\rm NS}$ given by semidefinite programs, $Γ$ is the tightest. We also prove that the previously introduced simulation lower bound $Σ^{-}(K)$ is exactly multiplicative and satisfies $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)\leqΓ(K)\leqΣ^{-}(K)\leqΓ(K)^2$. Using this multiplicativity, we show that neither $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\log_2Σ^{-}(K)$ nor its regularized extension $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\lim\nolimits_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log_2Σ^{-}(K^{\otimes n})$ holds in general. This answers an open question about the asymptotic simulation cost $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)$. For classical-quantum channels, we obtain sharp bounds. If $r$ is the effective output dimension, then $Θ_{\rm NS}\leqΓ\leq(1+r^{1/2})Θ_{\rm NS}/2$ and $Γ\leqΣ^{-}\leq(1+r^{1/2})Γ/2$. If $k$ is the minimum rank of the output support projections, then $Σ^{-}/Θ_{\rm NS}\leq[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]^2$, and this bound is sharp for every $1\leq k\leq r$. Thus, we obtain the sharp bound $S_{0,\rm NS}-C_{0,\rm NS}\leq2\log_2[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]$.

titles.title: Multiplicative Semidefinite Programming Upper Bounds on Quantum No-Signalling-Assisted Zero-Error Capacity

abstracts.value:
We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most 
\[ \exp[-Ω(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \]
 for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+δ$ is at most $\exp[-Ω(δ^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<δ\le\varepsilon$. Our information charge is the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. Our comparison states preserve the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

titles.title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy

abstracts.value: We study the problem of online learning of quantum states with logarithmic loss, which is a quantum generalization of online portfolio selection and has applications to quantum state tomography, the task of estimating an unknown quantum state from measurement outcomes. We first establish a regret lower bound, showing that the regret rates of Exponential Weights and the algorithm of Tseng et al. (2025) have optimal polynomial dependence on the dimension. Our analysis leads to two further results. First, our lower-bound proof leads to a quantum state tomography algorithm that is sample optimal up to polylogarithmic factors in the sample size. Second, we develop an algorithm for constructing confidence sequences for the mean of a matrix-valued random variable. A numerical experiment shows that the latter algorithm is competitive with existing methods.

abstracts.value: Recent studies have reported promising results from quantum machine learning in drug discovery, healthcare, materials science and cybersecurity. Research includes comparisons with classical machine learning algorithms and the development of sequential hybrid pipelines. We propose that fusion can improve prediction when classical and quantum representations capture complementary predictive relationships. Our classical-quantum multi-view framework preserves the full classical input alongside simulated quantum features. Concatenation and attention combine the views; single-view comparisons, replacement and masking controls assess both views' contributions. Controlled angular-polynomial experiments distinguish targets adequately represented by a single view from those that depend on complementary angular and polynomial relationships. For these mixed targets, fusion improves prediction by combining the relevant feature sets, while matched classical representations recover the same benefit, linking the improvement to their complementary predictive content. Controlled classification tests further show that gains depend on alignment between the chosen representation and the target, and on a suitable fusion rule. Benchmark validation shows improved mean predictive performance over classical baselines on Wine, Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer, three-class Fashion-MNIST and Steel Plates Faults within the evaluated protocols. Classical replacement and masking controls remain competitive, classical baselines lead on Digits and Covertype, and outcomes with missing or corrupted views depend on the available inputs. These findings support evaluating quantum representations for their complementary predictive contribution and matching the representation and fusion strategy to the target relationships.

titles.title: When do quantum views help? Complementary classical-quantum representations in multi-view fusion

abstracts.value: Preparing quantum states in bosonic qudits with SNAP--Displacement sequences requires both optimizing the gate parameters and deciding which Fock levels should be controlled by each SNAP gate. A fully parameterized ansatz assigns an independent phase to every Fock level in every gate, leading to a number of phases that grows steeply. This constitutes a problem for short to medium term systems as controlling many phases requires complex control pulses which are subject to increased control errors. Previous work reduced this cost by restricting the trainable phases to predefined sparse patterns, such as a diagonal or a grid, which however may not be optimal for a specific target state. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a method that learns which phases are needed together with their values, using a differentiable mask. A sparsity penalty encourages the removal of unnecessary phases, while temperature annealing gradually turns the masks into binary decisions. We compare the proposed method with fully parameterized and predefined sparse ansatzes on Fourier and Haar-random target states. The evaluation considers both the minimum number of phases required to reach different infidelity thresholds and the overall trade-off between fidelity and phases required, measured through Pareto frontiers and hypervolume. The results show that learning the location of the phases together with their values provides competitive or improved fidelity--resource trade-offs, although the advantage depends on the target state and qudit dimension.

titles.title: Reducing the Cost of Qudit State Preparation by Learning a Sparse Structure for SNAP Gates

abstracts.value: Together with a right-handed neutrino, the fermions of one generation of the Standard Model are labelled by five bits, a combinatorial structure tied to anomaly cancellation. We make this precise. Anomaly cancellation is the vanishing of a cubic form, the defining property of triorthogonal codes, the quantum error-correcting codes behind magic state distillation. Removing the right-handed neutrino gives a $[[15,1,3]]_p$ code for every prime $p$, including the Bravyi-Kitaev code for $p = 2$. For qutrits it is the unique shortest distance-three triorthogonal code.

titles.title: One generation of the Standard Model as a quantum error-correcting code

abstracts.value: Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native placement found no consistent advantage in correct-answer probability for either submission track, but did not establish equivalence between the tracks. Structural comparisons depend on metric weighting, placement and device generation. Provider interfaces also limit observability: Rigetti's supported-operation list remained unchanged across a device generation that replaced the native entangler. We classify silent interface failures in composed toolchains and identify checks at toolchain boundaries, connecting valid cross-provider comparisons with concrete software-quality practices.

titles.title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement

abstracts.value: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

titles.title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs

abstracts.value: Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.

titles.title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits

abstracts.value: Diffusion language models generate text by reversing a classical diffusion process over token sequences. We show that their continuous-time forward and reverse dynamics can be embedded in the framework of open quantum systems, which describes quantum systems interacting with their environment. This connection provides a basis for extending diffusion sampling to superpositions of sentence states and for modifying the underlying generation dynamics. We construct a $τ$-leaping unraveling scheme that simulates stochastic trajectories of these states while updating multiple token positions at each step. This enables generation conditioned on superposed prompts or thoughts, which we call Superposition of Prompts (SoP) and Superposition of Thoughts (SoT). The same formulation yields Quantum-Inspired Remasking (QIR): perturbing the masked-diffusion dynamics produces a confidence-based rule for revising previously generated tokens. Experiments with pretrained diffusion language models show that superposition-based generation can retain information from conditioning components not selected at the final measurement, while QIR improves LLM-assessed text quality when applied at an appropriate stage of generation.

titles.title: Diffusion Language Models as Open Quantum Systems

abstracts.value: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.

titles.title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation

abstracts.value: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

titles.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs

abstracts.value: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

titles.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

abstracts.value: Quantum collapse (QC) occurs under the action of the inverse-power potential U(r)=-U_0/(2r^n) in the framework of the Schroedinger equation. The corresponding stationary wave functions feature an infinite number of spatial oscillations at $r\rightarrow 0$. The ground state (GS) is missing in the presence of the QC, but the available bound states at finite energies may be physically relevant, as they are normalizable. This work aims to produce singular stationary wave functions. The analytical findings represent an asymptotic form of the stationary wave functions at $r\rightarrow 0$, which fill a continuous spectrum, and some exact solutions for the wave functions, obtained under appropriate conditions. As a regularized version, we also consider the potential truncated at a finite difference from the center. The regularized wave functions feature a finite number of spatial oscillations, the missing GS reappears, and the spectrum of the bound states is discrete.

titles.title: Singular wave functions and quantum collapse in inverse-power potentials

abstracts.value: We prove the formation of trapped surfaces for the Einstein--Euler system in 3+1 dimensions beyond spherical symmetry. We consider smooth characteristic initial data in a short-pulse regime with rapid fluid injection. Starting from initial data containing no trapped surfaces, we obtain two sufficient criteria for trapped surface formation, corresponding to the shear and fluid contributions, respectively. In particular, for the fluid-driven criterion, we impose no positive lower bound on the shear flux. To handle the multiple propagation speeds associated with gravitational waves, sound waves, and fluid transport, our analysis combines three ingredients: a coercive fluid energy current whose null fluxes reflect the unequal velocity components, curvature renormalizations adapted to the matter terms, and weighted geometric estimates controlling derivatives in all spacetime directions. To ensure that fluid injection alone can lead to trapped surface formation, we use particle-number conservation in a designed spacetime region to control the focusing process and obtain the desired sphere-integrated fluxes.

titles.title: Formation of Trapped Surfaces for the Einstein-Euler System

abstracts.value: We study the connection between the $SU(N)_{K}$ Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) model and $SU(N)_{K'}$ WZW models, enforcing the unbroken $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ symmetries. The fundamental underlying structures are the (half-)integer spin simple currents in the topological quantum field theories and anomaly matching conditions in conformal field theories. For the (half-)integer spin simple current condition of the folded models $SU(N)_{K}\boxtimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{N}} \overline{SU(N)_{K'}}$ or $SU(N)_{K}\boxtimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{N}} SU(N)_{K'}$, we obtain the generalized pairing condition $K= \pm R^{2}K' (\text{mod}.N)$ with $\text{gcd}(R,N)=1$. On the other hand, the anomaly matching condition results in the weaker condition $K= \pm RUK' (\text{mod}.N)$ with $\text{gcd}(R,N)=\text{gcd}(U,N)=1$. Surprisingly, the anomaly matching without the pairing condition results in the intrinsic mismatch of the preservation law of the $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ defects and symmetries. The pairing condition canonically relates symmetries and defects, as in category theory, whereas it is unclear whether it can be a guiding principle in prohibiting the massless renormalization group flows.

titles.title: Difference between pair creation and anomaly matching: Nontrivial aspects of invertible symmetries and defects in $SU(N)$ models

abstracts.value: We propose a general statistical framework for characterizing erratic functions through the statistics of their extrema, with the aim of identifying statistical signatures associated with chaotic processes. It is based on analyzing the extrema points of erratic functions associated with these processes. One is instructed to determine the probability distribution functions ( PDF)s of the locations of the extrema points, the spacings between the locations, in particular the nearest neighbors, and the ratios between adjacent spacings. We then fit these PDFs with PDFs known to relate to chaotic behavior like of random matrix theory. The extrema considered establish a cloud of points in general in $D$ dimensions for erratic function of several variables. For certain systems one finds also extrema curves. We further determine the ``thermodynamic" description of the erratic functions by computing the Shannon or differential entropy and by equating the PDFs to the Gibbs one. With this map we determine the ``energy function" and for certain cases also the ``temperature". We analyze three benchmark spacing PDFs: the Bernoulli shift map, the Poisson and the Gaussian beta ensemble and several others. We want to emphasize that the map to thermodynamics can be applied to variety of chaotic processes including non-physics ones. We distinguish marginal spacing distributions from joint distributions of consecutive spacings. The latter probe correlations and statistical organization that are invisible in one-spacing PDFs and may provide stronger signatures for distinguishing structured chaotic-like behavior from uncorrelated irregularity.

titles.title: Statistical Characterization of Erratic and Chaotic Processes through Their Extrema I. Thermodynamics

abstracts.value: We study the von Neumann operator-space entanglement entropy (OSEE) of initial product operators evolved under random gaussian dynamics, as modeled by a Brownian SYK$_2$ model. abstracts.value: Riemannian optimization provides a natural geometric framework for designing quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation, most notably through quantum imaginary-time evolution. However, existing geometry-aware approaches primarily employ steepest-descent updates, leaving more advanced methods from classical Riemannian optimization largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient that combines the steepest descent direction with information retained from previous search directions. In our numerical experiments, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence per iteration than the baseline double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm, and we quantify the associated circuit cost with gate counts produced by Qrisp. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of increased circuit depth for each update step, revealing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity. Nevertheless, since the circuit depth for those algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, the proposed method may offer practical advantages, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.

titles.title: Quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient for ground-state preparation

abstracts.value: We investigate a single-component Abelian-Higgs model with an eighth-order scalar potential whose vacuum manifold consists of two disconnected circles. The model supports two species of vortices and domain walls interpolating between the two vacuum components. We find type-1.5-like behavior characterized by nonmonotonic intervortex interactions and bound states of spatially separated vortices. Inner-vacuum vortices form clusters through short-range repulsion and long-range attraction, whereas outer-vacuum vortices form vortex-filled bubbles in which a closed domain wall confines multiple inner-vacuum-vortex cores. We construct the domain wall analytically, derive the asymptotic vortex-wall interactions, and analyze the fluctuation spectra of coincident multivortices to identify their splitting instabilities.

abstracts.value: The classical capacity of a noisy optical channel is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably, given a constraint on the mean input energy. For the ubiquitous bosonic Gaussian channels, which include standard models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links, determining this rate requires addressing whether entanglement between channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings. More precisely, the question is whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive across arbitrarily many channel uses and coincides with its Gaussian counterpart. We answer these fundamental questions in the affirmative for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Namely, we prove that independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the capacity, including in the low-energy regime where squeezing the signals competes with encoding information in their displacement. Our proof connects an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on output entropy. We then characterise communication above capacity: under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the probability of correct decoding decreases exponentially with the number of channel uses, and we derive explicit bounds on the decay exponent. When only the mean photon number is constrained, a simple energy-rescaling formula determines exactly the entire asymptotic rate--error trade-off: the capacity at mean photon number $N$ and allowed average decoding error $ε$ equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number $N/(1-ε)$. Together, these results identify the ultimate limits of classical communication for some of the most fundamental models of optical communication.

titles.title: Classical Capacity of Single-Mode Bosonic Gaussian Channels

abstracts.value: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

titles.title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction

abstracts.value: On a compact Riemann surface of genus $g \geq 2$, we study Simpson's stratification of the de Rham moduli space of rank-2 flat connections. Upon representing flat $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$-connections by branched projective structures, or equivalently by opers with apparent singularities, the stratum containing a flat connection is determined by the minimal number of apparent singularities needed to represent it. We construct explicit holomorphic families in which two simple apparent singularities collide and disappear, so that the family crosses into a smaller stratum; this realizes Simpson's closure relation between strata near generic points. The analogous families of Higgs bundles are described by Baker--Akhiezer divisors on the spectral curve in which two points converge to a pair of points exchanged by the spectral involution. We show that, before the collision, the two apparent singularities are joined by twin paths bounding a bubble, so that these families arise from the isomonodromic bubbling surgery discussed by Calsamiglia, Deroin and Francaviglia.

abstracts.value: In this work, we study vector field theories with spontaneous Lorentz violation induced by a nonderivative potential $V(X)$ (with $X = B_μB^μ$), known as bumblebee models, with a Maxwell kinetic term in Minkowski spacetime. We confirm a recent result showing that a class of smooth potentials, including a purely cubic potential, leads to a Hamiltonian density that is bounded from below and assumes a global minimum for nonzero timelike expectation values of the vector field satisfying $X = b^2 > 0$, inducing spontaneous Lorentz-symmetry breaking. We show explicitly that the standard quadratic potential has a Hamiltonian that is unbounded from below and thus unstable. We analyze the Hamiltonian equations of motion for the timelike case and demonstrate that they are regular at the global minimum. Furthermore, we examine the linearized spectrum of small fluctuations around the minimum. We also study particular solutions with spherical symmetry analytically and numerically, without assuming linearization. We find that the time evolution of smooth initial configurations can develop shock-like singularities, and we explain why this behavior is expected in this model. We also identify a subset of the space of field configurations in which the field equations cease to be hyperbolic, leading to a breakdown of well-posedness of the Cauchy initial-value problem.

titles.title: Stability and dynamics of bumblebee models

abstracts.value: Stars may become embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) accretion disks and eventually explode as supernovae (SNe), whose detection would provide direct evidence for the existence and evolution of stars in AGN disks. We investigate the electromagnetic emission of such disk SNe using an analytic shock dynamics model coupled with a one-zone radiation model. Applying this framework to four progenitor types over a range of AGN black hole masses and Eddington ratios, we find that disk SNe around lower-mass black holes (BHs) or at lower Eddington ratios are more readily detectable against the underlying AGN emission and can remain detectable over a broader range of electromagnetic bands, from the infrared to soft X-rays. However, detectability against the AGN background does not guarantee that disk SNe can be distinguished from isolated SNe with CSM interaction. We therefore further compare disk SNe with isolated SNe with and without CSM interaction and find substantial degeneracies in their macroscopic observables. Nevertheless, we identify distinctive signatures that are robust across progenitor types. The characteristic emission shifts from the EUV for \(M_{\rm BH}\lesssim10^7\,M_\odot\) toward the UV/optical for \(M_{\rm BH}=10^8\,M_\odot\), with the visibility timescale increasing from less than a day to \(\sim3\text{--}70\) days and \(T_{\rm peak}\sim3\text{--}8\) eV in the latter case. The UV/optical regime around \(10^8\,M_\odot\) BHs therefore offers particularly promising prospects for detecting disk SNe.

titles.title: Detecting and Identifying Supernovae in AGN Accretion Disks

abstracts.value: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

titles.title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors

abstracts.value: Distinguishing between dark energy and modified gravity as the origin of the accelerated expansion requires the cosmic distances and the growth of structure to be measured in a model-independent way. Such measurements are difficult to perform while the primordial shape parameters are varied at the same time, and those parameters are therefore usually held fixed at the values determined by cosmic microwave background experiments. In this work, we present a methodology that constrains the shape parameters simultaneously with the model-independent distance and growth parameters, using an emulator built upon a hybrid model in which perturbative predictions are supplemented by templates measured from $N$-body simulations. {Because these templates are measured rather than expanded, the model carries non-linear corrections beyond the order at which its perturbative part is truncated, so that its accuracy on small scales is set by the simulations rather than by the reach of the expansion.} A Gaussian process emulator supplies these templates rapidly across the space of scale-dependent parameters, which makes the joint analysis computationally feasible, and the emulator is trained and validated over a range spanning $5σ$ of the Planck constraints. Applying the method to the LRG2 sample of DESI DR1, we obtain measurements of the Alcock--Paczynski parameters $α_\perp$ and $α_{||}$ and of the growth rate $fσ_8$. {With the tight Planck prior adopted here the constraints differ from those obtained with the shape parameters held fixed by less than a twentieth of their own uncertainties, so that the choice of template contributes at that level to the error budget of the measurement. Projected onto flat $Λ$CDM after the fit, the three measurements are mutually consistent, with $χ^2=0.7$ for two degrees of freedom, and require $h=0.724\pm0.017$.}

titles.title: Model-independent parameters from DESI DR1 LRG2 with an explicitly varying power-spectrum shape
